title: Baldwin edges Lahainaluna 7–6, draws Saint Damien in state football opener
excerpt: The MIL champion Bears finish a three-game sweep of the Lunas and open the HHSAA Division I tournament Saturday. Kamehameha Maui is the top seed in Division II.
body:
The MIL champion Bears finish a three-game sweep of the Lunas and open the HHSAA Division I tournament Saturday. Kamehameha Maui is the top seed in Division II.

Baldwin beat Lahainaluna 7–6 in Maui Interscholastic League football on Saturday night, Nov. 7, at Sue D. Cooley Stadium in Lahaina, according to the Star-Advertiser scoreboard. The game was on Lahainaluna’s athletics calendar at Sue D. Cooley Stadium.

Three for three against the Lunas

It was the third Baldwin–Lahainaluna game of the season, and the Bears won all three. Baldwin won 27–19 on Sept. 18, then 13–3 at Lahainaluna on Oct. 16, the win that locked up the MIL Division I title and a state berth, according to The Maui News. Saturday’s one-point game was the closest of the three.

Baldwin came in 7–1 and Lahainaluna 3–5, according to MaxPreps, which puts the Bears at 8–1 and the Lunas at 3–6 after Saturday.

No box score or scoring summary had been posted for this game as of Tuesday morning, so we don’t have player stats yet. If you have them, send them our way.

Bears open state play Saturday on Oʻahu

The HHSAA Division I bracket has No. 5 Baldwin facing No. 4 Saint Damien on Saturday, Nov. 14, at 7:30 p.m. at Edward “Skippa” Diaz Stadium at Farrington High School. The winner plays at No. 1 Waipahu in the semifinals, and the Division I final is Saturday, Nov. 28, at 7:30 p.m. at John Kauinana Stadium at Mililani High School.

It’s a rematch of last year’s state opener. Baldwin’s 2025 season ended with a 28–14 loss to Damien at Farrington, The Maui News reported.

Kamehameha Maui is the No. 1 seed in Division II

Kamehameha Maui is the top seed in the HHSAA Division II bracket, so the Warriors skip the first round and host a semifinal on Friday, Nov. 20, at 6 p.m. at Kanaʻiaupuni Stadium. They’ll play the winner of Saturday’s No. 4 Kalaheo vs. No. 5 Pac-Five game (4 p.m. at Farrington). The Division II final is Saturday, Nov. 28, at 4 p.m. at Mililani.

Kamehameha Maui is 7–2 after its 26–13 homecoming loss to King Kekaulike on Nov. 6, according to KHON2. Read our story.

Getting tickets

The HHSAA says tickets for every state tournament game go on sale on GoFan the Sunday night before the game. Times and sites can change, so check with the HHSAA and the schools before you go. Our MIL Football Schedule 2026 guide has every result from this season and the state dates.

title: Keeping it fun: burnout and mental health for Maui’s young athletes
excerpt: Why so many kids walk away from sports, what burnout and overtraining look like, and simple ways Maui families and coaches can keep the game fun as fall seasons end and winter seasons begin.
body:
Why so many kids walk away from sports, what burnout and overtraining look like, and simple ways Maui families and coaches can keep the game fun as fall seasons end and winter seasons begin.

General information, not medical advice. If you’re worried about your child’s mood, sleep or energy, talk with their pediatrician or a mental health professional.

This is a big week of change for a lot of Maui families. Fall seasons are wrapping up after MIL and state championships, and winter sports and club seasons start right behind them. It’s a good moment to step back and ask a simple question: is my kid still having fun?

Why so many kids stop playing

The American Academy of Pediatrics says research shows about 70% of kids drop out of organized sports by age 13. A 2019 Aspen Institute Project Play survey of parents found the average child spends less than three years in a sport and quits by about age 11. The most common reason, 36% of the time, was that the child stopped enjoying it or lost interest. Only 15% of the time did a child quit to try a different sport.

Kids say the same thing in their own words. In a 2026 Project Play report built on a national survey of more than 3,800 young people ages 10 to 17, “having fun” (48%) and “playing with friends” (47%) were the top things current players love about sports. Only 12% put earning a college scholarship or roster spot among their favorites. Among kids who had quit, feeling “I’m not good enough” (29%) and “bad coaching” (21%) were the top complaints.

What burnout and overtraining look like

In its 2024 clinical report, the AAP describes burnout as physical or mental exhaustion and a reduced sense of accomplishment that leads a young athlete to stop valuing the sport. It calls burnout one of the main reasons kids leave youth sports.

Overtraining is related. The AAP describes it as a drop in performance from too much training and not enough recovery, often with ongoing tiredness, poor sleep and changes in mood. Too much training and an overloaded schedule are two possible risk factors for burnout, and the AAP notes it has become more common for young athletes to play on several teams at once and train year-round.

Signs worth noticing at home include:

  • Being tired all the time, even after rest days
  • Trouble sleeping
  • Mood changes, such as being more irritable or down than usual
  • Performance slipping even though they’re working hard
  • Dreading practice or no longer talking about a sport they used to love

It isn’t only about how many sports a child plays. “Whether training is specialized or multisport, it becomes a problem when an athlete no longer has any free play time or opportunity to engage in other non-sport-related activities,” Dr. Andrew Watson, a co-author of the report, said in the AAP’s announcement.

What helps

These ideas come from the AAP’s recommendations, with a few Maui-family touches:

  • Celebrate effort, not just the scoreboard. The AAP recommends measuring success by participation and effort. After a tough loss, “I loved watching you play” goes a long way on the drive home.
  • Leave room in the calendar. Avoid overscheduling and keep some unstructured time each week, whether that’s the beach, the backyard or just hanging out with friends.
  • Take real breaks. AAP authors encourage time away from sports. The gap between fall and winter seasons is a natural spot for a few days off.
  • Keep practice playful. The AAP suggests age-appropriate games to keep training interesting and fun, especially for younger keiki.
  • Stay involved in a positive way. In the 2026 Project Play survey, 86% of current players had parents who came to games or practices, compared with 58% of kids who had quit. Former players were also more than twice as likely to say they had been pressured to play when they didn’t want to (21% vs. 9%).
  • Start with a checkup. The AAP recommends a pre-participation exam with your child’s own doctor, who can look at the whole picture.

When it might be more than burnout

If you see signs of burnout or overtraining, the AAP advises changing what’s causing it and bringing in a mental health professional if needed. If your child seems sad or withdrawn for weeks, or ever talks about hurting themselves, reach out for help right away. You can call or text 988, the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, any time, day or night.

The bottom line

Sports are supposed to be good for kids, body and mind. In the 2026 survey, 81% of current players said their mental state gets better when they play. Keeping it fun, keeping the schedule sane and cheering for effort are some of the best ways to make sure our keiki keep playing for years.

Coaches, athletic trainers, counselors or health professionals on Maui with tips for young athletes and their families? Send them to us and we may feature them in a future story.

Sources:

American Academy of Pediatrics, HealthyChildren.org, “AAP Calls Out Causes of Overuse Injuries & Burnout in Youth Sports” (2024)

Cheerleading

Baldwin, Maui High and Lahainaluna all competed in the 12-team All-Girl division at the HHSAA state cheerleading championships on Wednesday, Nov. 4, at the Neal S. Blaisdell Center Arena in Honolulu. Baldwin finished 8th with a final score of 35.40 and no deductions. Maui High finished 10th at 31.62 after a raw score of 33.37 and 1.75 in deductions. The HHSAA state air riflery championships were Tuesday, Nov. 3, at the Neal Blaisdell Exhibition Hall. Scores are listed as points and inner tens.

Maui High’s boys finished 7th of 8 teams with 2017 points and 42 inner tens (664 kneeling, 745 prone, 608 standing), per the official boys team results. Dallas Bayez led the Sabers with 523 points (12 inner tens). Moanalua won the boys title with 2124-49, followed by Kaiser at 2109-54 and Pearl City at 2100-50.

Maui High’s girls finished 6th of 8 with 2016 points and 40 inner tens (675 kneeling, 753 prone, 588 standing). Hannah Cabebe led Maui High with 523 (13 inner tens). Baldwin’s girls finished 7th with 1951 points and 25 inner tens (648 kneeling, 722 prone, 581 standing), led by Raylee Ribucan with 507 (3 inner tens), according to the official girls team results. Punahou won the girls title with 2142-56, followed by Pearl City at 2134-51 and Kaiser at 2078-44.

Bowling

The HHSAA state bowling championships ran Thursday and Friday, Nov. 5–6, at Schofield Bowling Center. Team totals are eight-game pin counts from the official HHSAA team results.

Kamehameha Maui’s girls finished 9th of 9 with 4,239 pins (563, 543, 537, 530, 501, 536, 549, 480). Mililani won the girls title with 6,714, followed by Kalani at 6,454 and Mid-Pacific at 5,605.

Baldwin’s boys finished 8th of 10 with 5,671 pins (843, 731, 726, 714, 705, 603, 627, 722). Kamehameha Maui’s boys finished 9th with 5,534 pins (677, 661, 727, 679, 703, 667, 673, 747). Mililani won the boys title with 7,954, followed by Pearl City at 7,036 and Moanalua at 6,969.

Catching up: football, cross country and MIL cheer

We can now confirm a football final from the week before: King Kekaulike 48, Kūlanihākoʻi 7 on Saturday, Oct. 31, at King Kekaulike, according to MaxPreps and the Star-Advertiser scoreboard. King Kekaulike was 5–3 after that game, and Kūlanihākoʻi finished 0–8 with no more games scheduled (MaxPreps).

At the MIL cross country championships on Oct. 24 at Baldwin, Seabury Hall won the boys team title with 20 points. Silas Miller-Yoder won the boys race in 17:09, and Seabury swept the top four (Brady Punu 17:24, Remi Kuriger 17:57, Brendan Punu 17:58). Kamehameha Maui won the girls team title with 36 points, and Keilana Maldonado won the girls race in 20:19, ahead of Brooke Hoida of Kīhei Charter (20:32) and Ariceli Gonzales of King Kekaulike (20:55). Kūlanihākoʻi scored 69 points and won its first MIL Division II girls title, according to The Maui News. Read the Kūlanihākoʻi story.

At the HHSAA state meet on Oct. 31 at Hawaiʻi Preparatory Academy in Waimea, Seabury Hall finished 2nd in boys Division II with 44 points behind champion Hawaiʻi Prep (25). Miller-Yoder was 5th overall and 2nd in Division II in 17:40, and Brady Punu was 6th overall in 17:44, per the official HHSAA combined team results. In Division I, King Kekaulike’s boys were 10th of 16 with 239 points (Makoa Kapuniai, 19:25, 45th overall) and Maui High’s boys were 12th with 314 (Ian Madriaga, 20:00, 77th overall). Kamehameha Maui’s girls were 9th of 16 with 254 points; Maldonado ran 22:12 and was 19th overall, the top Maui County girl, with Hoida 22nd and Emily Kermode of King Kekaulike 29th. Maui High’s girls were 13th with 314 points (Jozea Sanchez-Cabrera, 25:09).

On Oct. 27, Baldwin won the MIL cheerleading championship at Baldwin High School with a score of 37.43. Maui High finished 2nd and Lahainaluna 3rd (their scores were not published), and those top three teams advanced to states, according to The Maui News. Read the MIL cheer story.

title: Kūlanihākoʻi wins its first MIL DII girls cross country title
excerpt: Kūlanihākoʻi made school cross country history at Baldwin on Oct. 24, earning its first MIL Division II girls championship with 69 points.
body:
Kūlanihākoʻi made school cross country history at Baldwin on Oct. 24, earning its first MIL Division II girls championship with 69 points.

A first championship gives a team a place in school history. For Kūlanihākoʻi’s girls cross country program, that milestone arrived Saturday, Oct. 24, at Baldwin High School: the school’s first Maui Interscholastic League Division II girls cross country title.

Kūlanihākoʻi finished with 69 points, third in the combined girls team standings and the Division II champion. The Maui News’ championship report identifies the win as the program’s first MIL DII girls title.

Seven runners, one team milestone

Lucy James led Kūlanihākoʻi with an eighth-place finish in 22 minutes, 2 seconds. Eva Starmer followed in 13th, and Reese Hendrickson was 16th. Here are the school’s seven finishers in the published girls results; places are overall, not Division II-only:

  • Lucy James: eighth, 22:02.
  • Eva Starmer: 13th, 23:38.
  • Reese Hendrickson: 16th, 24:01.
  • Amalia Starmer: 23rd, 24:23.
  • Kitelyn Shimada: 26th, 24:33.
  • Avery Alexander: 42nd, 26:51.
  • Olivia Schrandt: 45th, 27:06.

Where the title fits

The Division II championship and the combined meet standings tell different parts of the story. Kamehameha Maui had the lowest overall girls team score, 36 points, with Maui High second at 63. Kūlanihākoʻi’s 69 put it ahead of King Kekaulike’s 77.

The rest of the published team standings were Kīhei Charter, 129; Lānaʻi, 157; Molokaʻi, 177; and Lahainaluna, 235. Kamehameha Maui’s Keilana Maldonado won the individual race in 20:19.

For Kūlanihākoʻi families, the lasting result is a new milestone for this team: its first MIL Division II girls cross country championship. Congratulations to the runners and the school community celebrating it.

title: Student-athlete profile: Emmali Brash, Kamehameha Maui volleyball
excerpt: The Warriors junior put up 17 kills, 17 digs and 5 aces in Kamehameha Maui’s HHSAA Division I state tournament match.
body:
The Warriors junior put up 17 kills, 17 digs and 5 aces in Kamehameha Maui’s HHSAA Division I state tournament match.

title: Knee injuries in youth sports: a guide for Maui families
excerpt: Common knee injuries in taekwondo, martial arts, basketball, volleyball and soccer, the warning signs to watch for, when to see a doctor, how return to play works, and the training that helps prevent them.
body:
Common knee injuries in taekwondo, martial arts, basketball, volleyball and soccer, the warning signs to watch for, when to see a doctor, how return to play works, and the training that helps prevent them.

General information, not medical advice. If your child hurts a knee, talk with their pediatrician, a sports medicine doctor or an orthopaedic specialist.

Kicks, pivots, jump landings and sudden stops are part of what makes taekwondo, martial arts, basketball, volleyball and soccer fun. They also put a lot of load on the knee. Here’s what orthopaedic and pediatric experts say Maui families should know.

The common knee injuries

  • ACL sprains and tears. The ACL sits inside the knee and keeps the shinbone from sliding forward and the knee from rotating too far. The American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons (AAOS) lists the usual causes: quick changes of direction, sudden stops, slowing down from a run, landing wrong from a jump, and direct hits to the knee. Female athletes tear the ACL at 2 to 8 times the rate of males.
  • MCL sprains. The MCL runs along the inside of the knee. AAOS says it is one of the most commonly injured knee ligaments, usually from a force that pushes the knee sideways, like a blow to the outside of the knee or a hard twist.
  • Meniscus tears. The menisci are two rubbery cushions between the thigh and shin bones. In sports they often tear on a pivot or cutting move, sometimes along with an ACL injury, according to AAOS.
  • Kneecap pain. Patellofemoral pain syndrome is pain around the front of the kneecap. AAOS links it to overuse, to sudden jumps in how often or how hard a young athlete trains, and to weak or imbalanced thigh and hip muscles.
  • Growth-plate pain below the knee. Osgood-Schlatter disease causes a sore, sometimes swollen bump just below the kneecap in growing kids, most often during growth spurts and in running and jumping sports.

Why martial arts and court sports matter here

Spinning kicks, planted-foot pivots, sparring contact, jump serves and rebounds all involve the movements AAOS ties to ligament and meniscus injuries: twisting, cutting, landing and direct blows. That doesn’t mean these sports are unsafe. It means good technique, strong legs and an honest response to pain matter.

Warning signs

According to AAOS, watch for:

  • A “pop” at the moment of injury, or the knee giving out
  • Swelling, often within 24 hours for an ACL injury, or slowly building stiffness and swelling over 2 to 3 days with a meniscus tear
  • The knee catching, locking or feeling unstable
  • Not being able to fully bend or straighten the knee
  • Pain or limping when walking

One thing to know: with a meniscus tear, many athletes can still walk and even keep playing at first. Feeling “okay” right after a hit doesn’t rule out an injury.

When to see a doctor

Have a medical professional check the knee if your child heard or felt a pop, the knee swelled up, it gives way, locks or won’t straighten, or pain is still there after a few days of rest. Pain below the kneecap that keeps coming back during a growth spurt is worth a visit, too. Doctors usually start with a hands-on exam and may order X-rays or an MRI.

What recovery can look like

Recovery depends on which structure is hurt, how badly, and your child’s age and goals.

  • MCL sprains. AAOS says low-grade MCL injuries without other damage can usually be treated without surgery, using rest, ice, compression, a hinged brace and physical therapy.
  • Meniscus tears. Many don’t need immediate surgery. Tears in the outer part of the meniscus, which has a good blood supply, may heal or be repairable. Tears in the inner part can’t heal on their own.
  • ACL tears. The American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) says ACL injuries often require surgery, many months of rehab, or both, plus real time away from school and sports. In a young athlete an ACL tear is not a surgical emergency, so families have time to talk through options with the care team.
  • Osgood-Schlatter. AAOS says most cases improve with rest, ice, pain relievers and stretching and strengthening.

Safe return to play

Coming back is a step-by-step process, not a date on the calendar. AAOS describes regaining full range of motion and strength with a physical therapist first, then a gradual “functional progression” back to sport-specific moves once the doctor clears it. For a martial artist that means kicks, pivots and sparring come back in stages. For court and field players, it means cutting, jumping and full-speed play. Going back too soon can make the injury worse.

Prevention: warm-ups and strength work

The AAP reviewed studies of injury-prevention programs in soccer, basketball, volleyball and handball. The most effective programs combined:

  • Jump training (plyometrics) with coaching on how to land softly with knees in line, not caving inward
  • Strength work for the legs, hips and core
  • Doing the program both before and during the season

In girls under 18, those programs cut ACL injury risk by about 72%, and the AAP says starting in early to middle adolescence may work best. Balance drills alone may not be enough. Ask your coach or dojang whether warm-ups include landing and strength work, and build in rest so a sudden jump in training load doesn’t lead to overuse pain.

The bottom line

Most knee pain in young athletes can be managed when it’s caught early. Take swelling, locking and giving way seriously, get it checked, follow the rehab plan, and make strength and landing practice a regular part of training.

title: Sleep and recovery for young athletes: a guide for Maui families
excerpt: How much sleep keiki and teen athletes really need, what the research says about sleep and sports injuries, and simple ways to protect bedtime during a busy season.
body:
How much sleep keiki and teen athletes really need, what the research says about sleep and sports injuries, and simple ways to protect bedtime during a busy season.

General information, not medical advice. If your child has ongoing trouble sleeping, snores loudly or seems tired all the time, talk with their pediatrician.

Between practice after school, games under the lights, homework and a long ride home from the other side of the island, sleep is often the first thing young athletes give up. But sleep is when the body recovers and the brain resets. Here’s what pediatric and sleep experts say, and how Maui families can make room for it.

How much sleep do they need?

The American Academy of Sleep Medicine recommends, on a regular basis and counting total sleep in 24 hours:

  • Ages 6 to 12: 9 to 12 hours
  • Ages 13 to 18: 8 to 10 hours

Those recommendations are endorsed by the American Academy of Pediatrics. For a teen who has to be up at 6 a.m. for school, eight hours means being asleep by 10 p.m., and that can be hard after a late game.

Why teens struggle to fall asleep early

It isn’t just habit. The AAP explains that sleep-wake cycles start shifting up to two hours later at the start of puberty, right when school days start earlier. That’s why the AAP has pushed for middle and high schools to start class at 8:30 a.m. or later. A CDC study of the 2011–12 school year found that no public middle or high schools in Hawaiʻi started that late at the time, so early mornings are a long-standing reality for many island keiki.

Sleep and sports injuries

A 2014 study of 112 middle and high school athletes in grades 7 to 12 found that those who slept less than eight hours a night on average were 1.7 times more likely to have had an injury than those who slept eight hours or more. It was one school and the study shows a link, not proof that short sleep causes injuries. Still, the researchers concluded that encouraging young athletes to get enough sleep may help protect them.

The AAP also notes that regular lack of sleep can lead to irritability, trouble concentrating, headaches and low mood, while kids who sleep enough tend to have healthier immune systems and do better with school, behavior, memory and mental health. All of that shows up on the court and the field, too.

Simple ways to protect sleep during the season

These tips come from the AAP’s healthy sleep habits guide:

  • Keep a steady schedule. Aim for about the same wake-up time on school days and weekends.
  • Screens off an hour before bed. The AAP recommends turning off all screens at least an hour before bedtime and keeping TVs, tablets and phones out of the bedroom at night. Charging the phone in the kitchen helps.
  • Make the bedroom sleep-friendly. Dim the lights before bed and keep the room at a comfortable temperature, which matters on warm Maui nights.
  • Watch the calendar. Practices, games, lessons and homework can stack up. Build in downtime so keiki can wind down.
  • Get outside and get bright light in the morning. Daytime activity and morning light help the body’s clock.
  • Be the example. Making sleep a family priority shows kids it’s part of being healthy, just like eating well and training hard.

When to check with the doctor

The AAP lists common sleep problems to watch for, including trouble falling asleep, waking up often at night, snoring, loud or heavy breathing while sleeping, and sleep apnea. If a teacher mentions your child is “zoning out” or falling asleep in class, that’s worth a conversation with your pediatrician. Most sleep problems are very treatable.

The bottom line

Rest isn’t the opposite of training. It’s part of it. A young athlete who gets enough sleep is better set up to learn, play, heal and enjoy the game.

title: Concussions in youth sports: what Maui parents should know
excerpt: How to spot a possible concussion, when to call 911, why “when in doubt, sit them out” matters, and how the step-by-step return to play works for keiki and teen athletes.
body:
How to spot a possible concussion, when to call 911, why “when in doubt, sit them out” matters, and how the step-by-step return to play works for keiki and teen athletes.

General information, not medical advice. If you think your child has a concussion, get them checked by a doctor or other health care provider. For any danger sign listed below, call 911.

MIL football is in its final weeks and state tournament games are on the calendar this month, so it’s a good time for a refresher on head injuries. Concussions aren’t just a football thing, either. They can happen in volleyball, soccer, basketball, surfing, skating or a tumble on the playground. Here’s what the CDC, the American Academy of Pediatrics and international sports medicine experts tell families.

What a concussion is

The CDC describes a concussion as a type of traumatic brain injury. It can come from a bump, blow or jolt to the head, and also from a hard hit to the body that makes the head snap back and forth. That quick motion can cause chemical changes in the brain, which is why a child may think, feel, learn, act or sleep differently afterward.

The CDC says most kids feel better within two to four weeks, though some have symptoms that last much longer. A history of earlier concussions, or more severe symptoms right after the injury, raises the chance of a longer recovery.

Signs to watch for

One of the trickiest parts: the CDC notes that signs may not show up right away and can take hours or even days to appear. For school-age keiki and teens, watch for a child who:

  • Seems dazed, stunned or confused about what just happened
  • Has sudden trouble remembering things or paying attention
  • Answers questions more slowly than usual
  • Looks clumsy or unsteady on their feet
  • Throws up soon after the hit
  • Shows changes in mood, behavior or personality

Kids may also say they have a headache, feel dizzy or sick to their stomach, or are bothered by light or noise. You know your child best. If something seems off, trust that.

When to call 911

The CDC lists danger signs that need emergency care right away, including a seizure, not recognizing people or places, vomiting again and again, getting more confused, restless or agitated, or losing consciousness. If you see any of these after a hit to the head or body, call 911 or go straight to the nearest emergency room.

When in doubt, sit them out

The CDC’s advice for a suspected sports concussion is simple: take the athlete out of the game or practice right away, keep them out for the rest of that day, and don’t let them return until a health care provider says it’s OK. Parents and coaches shouldn’t try to judge how bad it is on the sideline. The CDC says athletes who go back too soon, while the brain is still healing, have a greater chance of another concussion.

When you see the doctor, it helps to share how the injury happened, whether your child blacked out and for how long, any memory loss or seizure right after, how many concussions they’ve had before, and any medicines or natural remedies they take.

Recovery is about school and life, too

The American Academy of Pediatrics points out that concussion symptoms often get in the way of school, friends, family life and sports, and can affect a young athlete’s emotional well-being. The AAP says every concussion is different, so care should fit the individual child. It also says the main treatment is cutting back, not necessarily stopping, physical and thinking activities while the brain heals. Let teachers know, and ask the doctor about any short-term help at school.

Getting back in the game, one step at a time

The CDC’s 6-step return to play progression is based on the 2022 international consensus on concussion in sport. An athlete starts only after a health care provider gives the green light, and each step usually takes at least 24 hours:

  1. Back to regular activities, like school
  2. Light aerobic activity, such as walking or an easy bike ride
  3. Moderate activity, like jogging or lighter weight training
  4. Hard non-contact work, like sprints and sport drills
  5. Full-contact practice
  6. Games

If symptoms come back at any step, the CDC says to stop, contact the provider, and once symptoms are gone, start again at the step before. If your child’s school has a certified athletic trainer, work closely with them through this process.

Helmets help, but they’re not magic

The CDC is clear that there’s no such thing as a concussion-proof helmet. A helmet can help protect against serious head injuries when it fits properly, is in good shape, is certified for the sport, is the right one for your child’s age and is worn correctly every time. Even with a helmet, avoiding hits to the head is still the goal.

A quick checklist for families

  • Learn the signs, and remember they can show up hours or days later.
  • Teach keiki to speak up if they feel “off” after a hit. It isn’t letting the team down.
  • If a concussion is possible, sit out right away and stay out until a provider clears them.
  • Know the danger signs that mean calling 911.
  • Follow the step-by-step return, and go back a step if symptoms return.
  • Check helmet fit at the start of every season.

Aloha Volleyball Association is holding tryouts for its 2026–27 high school girls indoor club team on Sunday, Nov. 8, at South Maui Gym in Kīhei.

Got a high school volleyball player who wants more time on the court after the school season? Aloha Volleyball Association (AVA) has posted tryouts for its 2026–27 high school girls indoor club, and sign-ups are open now.

Tryout details

  • When: Sunday, Nov. 8, 10:45 a.m. to 12:15 p.m.
  • Where: South Maui Gym, 1501 Liloa Dr., Kīhei
  • Who: High school girls. The sign-up form includes AVA’s player age definition, so check it before you register.
  • Sign up: on AVA’s tryout sign-up form.

Both forms are on AVA’s Indoor Club page: the AVA waiver (PDF) and the medical release form (PDF). Filling them out ahead of time saves a scramble at the gym door.

What club volleyball costs

AVA is upfront that club play has three costs: club dues, a uniform and travel. Its Indoor Club page puts the uniform at about $150 to $225. Travel depends on how many players go. AVA estimates $800 to $1,200 per player for an outer-island trip and $1,500 to $2,000 for a Mainland trip, not counting airfare, which families cover. Dues vary by skill level, travel and season length, so ask the club for the current amount.

About AVA

AVA is a 501(c)(3) nonprofit that has been promoting volleyball in Maui County since 2004, through training, competitions and work on local courts, including nets and equipment for county sand courts, according to its About page. It also runs youth volleyball for ages 7 to 10.

Questions? AVA asks families to email info@alohavolleyball.com.

A year of waiting

The win flips last season’s ending. Kamehameha Maui beat King Kekaulike in five sets for the 2025 league title, according to The Maui News, and came into this season as the defending champion.

It was King Kekaulike’s second win over the Warriors in eight days, after a 3–1 win in their regular-season meeting on Oct. 13. The MaxPreps schedule now shows a seven-match winning streak for the Nā Aliʻi.

How they got here

King Kekaulike swept Lahainaluna 3–0 in Monday’s semifinal, and Kamehameha Maui swept Maui High 3–0 in the other. Lahainaluna had reached the semifinals by beating Baldwin in Saturday’s play-in. Catch up on the first rounds of the playoffs.

title: Fueling keiki athletes: a parent’s guide to food and drinks for youth sports
excerpt: What the research says about everyday meals, game-day food, water versus sports and energy drinks, supplements, and why eating enough matters for young athletes on Maui.
body:
What the research says about everyday meals, game-day food, water versus sports and energy drinks, supplements, and why eating enough matters for young athletes on Maui.

General information, not medical advice. Every keiki is different. Talk with your child’s doctor, athletic trainer or a registered dietitian before making changes, especially if your child has a health condition, food allergy or special diet.

No games to report today, so we’re looking at something that matters every day of the season: what our keiki eat and drink. Between after-school practice, weekend tournaments and Maui’s heat, young athletes need steady fuel. Here’s what the major medical and sports-health groups say.

Start with everyday meals

Good sports nutrition isn’t really about one special pregame meal. A joint position paper from the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics, Dietitians of Canada and the American College of Sports Medicine says performance and recovery both improve with well-chosen nutrition, meaning the right type, amount and timing of food and fluids. In practice that means regular meals and snacks with a mix of carbohydrates, protein, fruits and vegetables, built around the family’s normal food. Rice, poi, ʻulu, sweet potato, fish, chicken, eggs, tofu and local fruit all fit.

The same paper recommends that athletes who want a personal plan see a registered dietitian. That’s a good option for teens in heavy training or anyone with specific concerns.

Eating enough is a safety issue

The most common problem in youth sports isn’t eating the “wrong” food. It’s not eating enough for how much a child trains. The International Olympic Committee’s 2023 consensus statement describes Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (REDs): health and performance problems that happen in both girls and boys when food intake doesn’t keep up with exercise. The statement also points to links between REDs and mental health.

For parents and coaches, that means avoiding pressure about weight or body size, and paying attention if a young athlete is skipping meals, constantly tired, getting hurt often or losing interest in a sport they love. Those are reasons to check in with a doctor.

Water first

For most practices and games, water is the go-to drink. The American Academy of Pediatrics warns that sports drinks and energy drinks are often marketed to kids for the wrong reasons. It says the caffeine and other stimulants in energy drinks have no place in the diet of children and teens, and that drinking sugary sports drinks often or in large amounts can raise the risk of overweight and obesity.

The AAP report treats sports drinks and energy drinks as very different products. Sports drinks may have a role for athletes in long or high-intensity activity, but that’s a question for your child’s doctor or athletic trainer. Energy drinks don’t belong in the cooler.

Hydration in Maui heat

The National Athletic Trainers’ Association says athletes need easy access to water to avoid becoming dehydrated, but it also warns that drinking far too much can be harmful. Its advice is to plan fluids before, during and after activity that are enough but not excessive, and it notes that habits improve when water is easy to get and kids know why it matters.

Heat is a separate risk. NATA’s position statement on exertional heat illnesses calls exertional heat stroke one of the leading causes of sudden death in sport and urges teams to have an emergency plan at every venue. Practical steps for families: send a full, labeled water bottle to every practice, ask coaches about water breaks and shade, and know that hydration is only one part of staying safe in the heat.

Supplements: usually not needed

Protein powders, pre-workout mixes and other products are easy to find online. The AAP reviewed performance-enhancing substances in young athletes and raised concerns about high rates of product contamination and a link with later steroid use. It also found that for most young athletes, these products don’t add meaningful gains beyond the natural growth of puberty plus good food and training.

A simple checklist for families

  • Three meals a day plus snacks on training days. Don’t skip breakfast before school and afternoon practice.
  • Pack a snack for the drive home after practice. Long days on Maui roads add up.
  • Water bottle every day. Skip energy drinks entirely.
  • Check with a doctor or registered dietitian before buying supplements.
  • Watch for tiredness, frequent injuries or worry about weight, and speak up early.

Coaches, athletic trainers or dietitians on Maui with tips for keiki athletes? Send them to us and we may feature them in a future story.

Sources:

Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics, Dietitians of Canada and American College of Sports Medicine, “Nutrition and Athletic Performance” (2016)

American Academy of Pediatrics, “Sports Drinks and Energy Drinks for Children and Adolescents: Are They Appropriate?” (2011)

American Academy of Pediatrics, “Use of Performance-Enhancing Substances” (2016)

National Athletic Trainers’ Association, “Fluid Replacement for the Physically Active” (2017)

National Athletic Trainers’ Association, “Exertional Heat Illnesses” (2015)

International Olympic Committee consensus statement on Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (REDs), British Journal of Sports Medicine (2023)

This article is general information, not medical advice. Talk with a health professional about your child’s needs.

title: Catching up: Hāna scores 20 in the fourth to shut out Lānaʻi
excerpt: Hāna and Lānaʻi were scoreless through three quarters before the Dragons scored 20 straight in the fourth for a 20–0 eight-player football win on Oct. 2.
body:
Hāna and Lānaʻi were scoreless through three quarters before the Dragons scored 20 straight in the fourth for a 20–0 eight-player football win on Oct. 2.

One more early-October result for the record books, and it was a nail-biter until the very end.

Hāna hosted Lānaʻi in an eight-player MIL football game on Friday, Oct. 2, and neither team could find the end zone for three full quarters. Then the Dragons’ defense broke it open. An interception returned for a touchdown, plus a two-point conversion, gave Hāna an 8–0 lead. A second defensive score, this time on a fumble recovery, made it 14–0 after the two-point try came up short. A 6-yard touchdown run finished off the 20–0 shutout, according to The Maui News.

The two teams met again eight days later on Lānaʻi, and Hāna won that one too, 36–20. Read our recap of the rematch.
